summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focused on INT8 and FP8 quantization profiles, tradeoffs between quality and latency, and pilot next steps. Customer concerned about p95 latency for clinical chat and model quality regressions. Agreement to run Atlas sample prompts across profiles and set up a Dedicated pilot.
topics: Benchmarking methodology and metrics (p50/p95, perplexity, ROUGE-like QA accuracy)
Hosted vs Dedicated for predictable latency
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE. Priya and Daniel from our infra team will walk through Optimize quantization profiles - INT8, FP8, and how quality vs latency looks.
[00:14] Maya Patel: Hi all, Maya here. We care about p95 latency under 400ms for clinical chat, and quality can't drop more than 2% on our QA pass rates.
[00:23] Jordan Lee: Jordan, infra. We're evaluating Dedicated vs hosted - predictability is big for us.
[00:28] Priya Singh: Awesome, thanks. I'll share my screen - sorry if the auto-transcript messes up any of the model names, it sometimes writes FP-eight.
[00:36] [00:36] Priya Singh: Ok jumping in. We'll start with a quick primer: INT8 quantization generally gives bigger latency and memory wins for transformer MLPs, but FP8 can sometimes preserve more numeric fidelity for attention; depends on model and the quantization-aware ops.
[00:52] [00:52] Priya Singh: Here's a baseline: unquantized FP32 on our reference 8k token encoder model, p95 480ms on this hardware. INT8 profile hit p95 ~260ms, FP8 profile p95 ~300ms.
[01:08] Maya Patel: Wait, those numbers are on what hardware?
[01:11] Priya Singh: Good point - these were on A100s with our optimized kernels. For Atlas we'd run on T4s or A10s in Dedicated - Jordan, I know you're looking at A10s?
[01:21] Jordan Lee: We're leaning A10s for cost but might burst to A100. Latency numbers for A10s?
[01:25] Priya Singh: On A10s similar relative delta: unquantized p95 720ms, INT8 380ms, FP8 420ms. There's some variance due to kernel support.
[01:36] [01:36] Daniel Cho: Quick note - we've seen KV cash hits (transcript: KV cash) improve p50 massively for chat because of prefix reuse, but p95 is more about attention compute for long tails.
[01:50] Maya Patel: How do you measure "quality" here? Our QA is a mix of exact-match and clinician-graded scores.
[01:57] Priya Singh: We use a few signals: automated QA accuracy on prompt sets, token-level perplexity when applicable, and human evals sampled. For this walkthrough we ran Atlas-like prompts - medical QA and triage - and measured delta from FP32 baseline.
[02:12] [02:12] Priya Singh: Example: INT8 had a mean QA delta -1.1% vs FP32, FP8 -0.4% on our sample set. Those are averages; some prompts see higher variance.
[02:24] Sanjay Rao: That -1.1% could be material for us on edge cases. What's the distribution?
[02:29] Priya Singh: Right - tails matter. For critical safety-sensitive prompts, we typically suggest running a targeted eval set. We can flag prompts that regress beyond your threshold and keep those on FP32 or FP16. Our rollout supports per-route model variants.
[02:43] [02:43] Speaker 1: Is there an easy way to do per-route fallbacks?
[02:46] Daniel Cho: Yes. In Console you can set routing policies: if quantized model returns low confidence or fails a quality check, route to the fallback model. We showed this in the Optimize UI earlier - but we'll demo config.
[02:58] [02:58] Maya Patel: What's the expected cost delta? INT8 vs FP8 vs FP32?
[03:03] Alex Martinez: Ballpark: INT8 often reduces cost per token ~2.5-3x vs FP32, FP8 around 2x depending on throughput and GPU. That locks in if you can accept the small quality delta.
[03:17] Jordan Lee: For SLA we need predictable p95. Does Dedicated guarantee p95 in SLAs?
[03:23] Alex Martinez: Our Dedicated offering provides uptime and latency targets per contract; we can design the pilot with target SLOs and baseline load tests. For strict p95 SLOs we recommend overprovisioning and burst capacity.
[03:34] [03:34] Priya Singh: Back to benchmarks - here's a chart we ran: x-axis prompt length, y-axis p95 latency. You can see INT8 curve below FP8 and FP32 across the board, but the gap narrows at very long sequences because attention and KV I/O dominate.
[03:51] Maya Patel: Do you support mixed precision in inference? Like keep attention in FP32 and quantize MLP?
[03:57] Priya Singh: We do hybrid profiles - selective quantization. That often gives the best quality/latency tradeoff. It's in the Optimize recommendations as a profile: e.g., quantize MLP to INT8, keep attention in FP16/FP32.
[04:10] Sanjay Rao: And how much engineering is required on our side to adopt these profiles? We want minimal changes to our inference calls.
[04:17] Daniel Cho: Minimal - the API call stays the same. On Dedicated we manage model artifacts and runtime config. You pick a profile in Console or via API and we route to the binary with appropriate kernel picks. You'll get model artifacts (profile metadata) but not changes to client code.
[04:34] [04:34] Priya Singh: One gotcha: if you use custom ops or a finetuned model with fused kernels, sometimes quantization needs a short regeneration step; we can automate that in the onboarding POC.
[04:47] Maya Patel: For our clinical data, encryption and KMS are mandatory. How does quantization affect encrypted models or key management?
[04:54] Alex Martinez: No effect on KMS - quantized artifacts are still encrypted at rest and keys managed via your KMS/HSM. We can include audit logs for every deploy.
[05:05] Jordan Lee: Can you share an example CSV of latency/quality per-prompt?
[05:08] Priya Singh: Yes - action item. We'll run your sample set and return a CSV with columns: prompt_id, length, fp32_quality, int8_quality, fp8_quality, fp32_p95, int8_p95, fp8_p95, notes.
[05:21] [05:21] Maya Patel: That'll help. Also, do you support FP8 variants - e4m2 vs e5m2 or is that internal?
[05:28] Priya Singh: We expose some FP8 encodings as part of profile metadata. Our Optimize UI labels them - FP8-e4m3, etc. For most users we abstract that away and present expected quality deltas.
[05:40] Sanjay Rao: Regarding fallbacks - what's the latency penalty if we fall back from quantized to FP32 on a per-request basis?
[05:47] Daniel Cho: Fallback is a separate call; if you need synchronous fallback it adds network hop plus full FP32 latency. We often recommend an async retry path for heavy requests, or a canary route that keeps a small percentage on FP32.
[06:02] [06:02] Speaker 1: You mentioned KV cache earlier; can you quantify how much KV caching helps for our chat workload?
[06:07] Priya Singh: With strong prefix reuse, we've seen token-cost savings up to 30-50% and p50 latency ~2-3x improvement. p95 improvement is smaller unless you combine caching with request-level batching.
[06:20] Maya Patel: If we run a pilot, can we test both INT8 and FP8 and compare on our dataset?
[06:25] Priya Singh: Absolutely, that's the plan. We'll spin up two model variants in Dedicated pilot and run parallel A/B testing. We'll instrument quality checks to flag any regression above your threshold.
[06:36] Alex Martinez: We'll also include cost projections based on your observed throughput.
[06:40] [06:40] Jordan Lee: On the Dedicated specifics: what's the expected provisioning lead time?
[06:45] Alex Martinez: Typically 2-3 weeks for a Dedicated cluster depending on region and hardware; for pilot we try to use flexible Dedicated pools to shorten it to about a week if the hardware's available.
[06:55] Sanjay Rao: Ok. Are there known model families that don't quantize well? like some LLaMA variants?
[07:01] Priya Singh: Some highly fused, heavily-attenuated variants or models with custom kernels can be trickier. LLaMA derivatives generally quantize well, but if your finetune includes custom layers we may need a short retrace. We will surface warnings in the Optimize report.
[07:16] [07:16] Maya Patel: Could you show the Console UI profile recommendation?
[07:19] Priya Singh: Sure - now sharing. In the UI you pick workload type (chat vs generation vs embedding), target SLO, and Optimize suggests a ranked list of profiles with expected p95, cost multiplier, and sample quality delta.
[07:33] [07:33] Priya Singh: For Atlas we selected chat profile: INT8-fast, FP8-balanced, and Hybrid-safe. The UI gives a simulated cost and shows which prompts in your test set would likely regress beyond 1%.
[07:46] Jordan Lee: How confident are those simulations? do they come from real runs or heuristics?
[07:51] Priya Singh: They come from a mix: our offline runner (we re-run the model with quantized weights in our infra), plus heuristics based on architecture. Confidence is higher when we have real-run data; that's why the pilot is important.
[08:04] Maya Patel: We also need to check model explainability for audits. Does quantization affect attribution or saliency methods?
[08:12] Daniel Cho: The outputs are functionally equivalent but floating point changes can affect gradient-based attributions. For auditing, we recommend keeping a FP32 reference dataset and ground truth for critical paths.
[08:26] [08:26] Priya Singh: If you run into inconsistent attributions, we can isolate a set of probes and keep them on FP32 as a safety net.
[08:35] Sanjay Rao: What's the rollback experience? If a quantized rollout causes regressions in production, how fast can we roll back?
[08:41] Alex Martinez: Very fast - Console allows immediate rollback to previous model variant; with routing policies you can also redirect a percentage of traffic back within minutes. The actual time is bounded by your deploy window and replication across Dedicated nodes, typically under 10 minutes for a standard rollout.
[08:58] Maya Patel: Any privacy concerns with sending our sample prompts to Redwood for benchmarking? We can pseudonymize but prefer on-prem testing.
[09:05] Alex Martinez: We support private pilots - we have a private deployment option where your data and telemetry remain in your VPC. For initial benchmarking we can also run tests in an encrypted bucket with limited retention; we'll sign an NDA if needed.
[09:19] [09:19] Jordan Lee: Great. On measuring quality, can you export human evaluation forms from the Console for our clinicians to score?
[09:25] Priya Singh: Yes, Optimize can produce CSVs and a small UI for human-in-the-loop reviews. We can integrate your clinician graders or use our annotator network with blinded comparisons.
[09:36] Maya Patel: Cost-wise, if we do hybrid selective quantization, is that more expensive operationally?
[09:42] Daniel Cho: Slightly more complex in runtime but usually still cheaper than pure FP32. The net cost depends on fraction of critical requests pinned to FP32. Our recommendations will show cost at various split percentages.
[09:56] [09:56] Priya Singh: Moving into a concrete example - here's a slide with three prompts. Prompt A is short triage: INT8 and FP8 both preserved correctness; Prompt B is long differential diagnosis where INT8 showed a small hallucination 2% worse than FP32; FP8 preserved it. Prompt C is a toxic content filter test where both passed.
[10:16] Maya Patel: That hallucination is concerning. Can we tune quantization so it doesn't cause that?
[10:20] Priya Singh: Yes - options: hybrid profile, selective per-layer quantization, or keep small set of prompts on FP32. Also you can conserve higher precision for attention layers tied to factual recall.
[10:34] [10:34] Speaker 1: Is there an automated way to find these risky prompts?
[10:37] Priya Singh: Optimize includes a regression detection flow: you run a profile across your test set and it flags prompts with relative score drops beyond a configurable threshold. That list becomes your safety set.
[10:48] Jordan Lee: For the pilot, do you need us to provide infra access or do you want to manage everything?
[10:54] Alex Martinez: For Dedicated we typically provision clusters in Redwood-managed infra but can place within your cloud account or VPC if you prefer. For faster pilot we can start in Redwood-managed Dedicated with strict network controls.
[11:07] Sanjay Rao: One more on metrics: do you support p99 heatmaps or only p95?
[11:12] Daniel Cho: We collect p50/p95/p99 and full latency distributions. In Console you can view heatmaps and request traces.
[11:20] [11:20] Maya Patel: Ok this is helpful. Can you share a sample benchmark CSV now?
[11:24] Priya Singh: I'll attach the sample we've been referencing to the follow-up email; it's anonymized. For your dataset we'll run a fresh job.
[11:33] Alex Martinez: Quick recap before Qs: Run Atlas sample set on INT8/FP8/FP32, share CSV and UI report, spin Dedicated pilot with two model variants, share pricing and SOC2/KMS docs.
[11:46] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Two quick clarifying questions - will the Dedicated pilot include burst to A100s?
[11:52] Alex Martinez: We can include burst as an add-on. We'll include options in pricing.
[11:58] Jordan Lee: And final: how do we handle model updates during pilot? auto-roll or manual?
[12:03] Priya Singh: Manual by default; can be automated once you trust the profiles. We also support canary rollouts.
[12:11] [12:11] Sanjay Rao: Thanks. Any legal or procurement gating we should expect?
[12:16] Alex Martinez: Usually an enterprise procurement review for Dedicated; we'll start with standard MSA and SOW for pilot. Our legal can fast-track pilot agreements.
[12:26] Maya Patel: Alright let's set dates - we'll send the prompt set and target SLOs today.
[12:31] Alex Martinez: Great. We'll aim to deliver the benchmark CSV by 2026-03-30 and pricing by 2026-03-27.
[12:40] [12:40] Priya Singh: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the report and next steps.
[12:45] Speaker 1: Thanks all.
[12:48] [12:48] End of recording.

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription errors (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache, "FP-eight"), speaker labels include a generic "Speaker 1" in the customer group, and timestamps are approximate. The transcript aligns to a ~52-minute meeting with many sections removed for brevity in this export.
